# Reconstructing Images from WiFi Signals: The Full Story

### A plain-language walkthrough of what we built, what broke, why it broke, and what we actually learned

---

> **Who this is for:** a friend, classmate, or future version of yourself who wants to
> understand this project properly — not just the final number, but *why* the numbers
> mean what they mean, what nearly fooled us along the way, and what an honest, rigorous
> "it kind of works, here's exactly how much" result looks like in practice.
>
> Every technical term is explained the first time it shows up, and again in the glossary
> at the end. No prior machine learning background assumed.

---

## TL;DR, if you only read one paragraph

We tried to reconstruct an image of a room — showing where a person is and roughly what
shape they're in — using nothing but WiFi signal measurements, no camera. Our first few
attempts *looked* successful by the numbers, but turned out to be fooling us: the model was
taking a shortcut and not really "seeing" the person at all. Once we built better checks to
catch that shortcut, we found that a single instant of WiFi signal genuinely carries almost
no information about a person's position — but a short *window* of consecutive signal
readings, combined with more training examples from multiple people, does carry a real,
measurable, if modest, signal. That's the actual, defensible finding of this project.

---

## Part 1 — The Idea

### 1.1 What is WiFi CSI, really?

Every time a WiFi router and a device talk to each other, the signal travels through the
air and bounces off everything in the room — walls, furniture, and people. By the time it
arrives, it's been distorted in a very specific, measurable way depending on what it
bounced off.

**Channel State Information (CSI)** is the technical name for a detailed record of exactly
*how* that signal got distorted — captured as two things for every tiny frequency slice
the WiFi hardware uses:

- **Amplitude**: how much the signal's strength changed (like volume).
- **Phase**: how much the signal's timing shifted (like whether a wave arrived a little
  early or late compared to what was expected).

Modern WiFi doesn't send one signal — it splits data across roughly a hundred mini-frequencies
at once, called **subcarriers**, and CSI records amplitude and phase separately for each
one. That's what makes CSI rich enough to *potentially* carry spatial information: a person
standing in one spot disturbs different subcarriers differently than a person standing
somewhere else.

### 1.2 Why try to turn this into an image at all?

Cameras have two obvious weaknesses: they need light, and they raise privacy concerns
(a camera in a bedroom is invasive; a WiFi router isn't). If CSI genuinely encodes where a
person is and what shape they're in, then in principle you could get camera-like spatial
awareness — for things like fall detection or occupancy sensing — from hardware that's
already sitting in every house.

That's the premise. This project set out to test it, honestly, rather than assume it.

---

## Part 2 — The Dataset

### 2.1 MM-Fi

We used a public research dataset called **MM-Fi**, which recorded WiFi CSI *at the same
time* as several other sensors (cameras, depth cameras, radar, LiDAR) watching 40 different
people perform 27 different actions each, across several rooms. The "at the same time" part
matters enormously: it means every WiFi reading has a matching, verified answer — what the
room actually looked like at that exact instant — which is what lets you train and check a
model at all.

We didn't use every sensor MM-Fi offers. Two we tried:

- **`ground_truth.npy`**: for every action, a file containing the 3D position of 17 body
  joints (head, shoulders, elbows, knees, etc.) for all ~297 recorded instants. This is
  what's called a **keypoint** or **pose** representation — a skeleton, not a photo.
- **`depth/*.png`**: real depth-camera images — grayscale pictures where brightness
  represents *distance from the camera*, not color. Unlike a keypoint skeleton, this is a
  real, dense image showing the whole room, with the person visible as a silhouette.

> 📖 **A surprise worth flagging:** MM-Fi's `rgb/` folder does *not* contain photos. For
> privacy reasons, real camera photos are anonymized/restricted, and what ships by default
> in that folder is actually a second set of keypoints extracted from a camera view — not
> pixels. We only discovered this by actually inspecting the files directly rather than
> trusting the folder name; a useful lesson repeated several times in this project (see
> Part 7).

### 2.2 Widar3.0 (considered, not used)

We briefly considered a second public dataset, **Widar3.0**, which has WiFi CSI paired with
hand-gesture labels. We ultimately didn't use it, because it has no paired image or
keypoint data at all — it can tell a model "this was a push gesture," but not "here's what
the room looked like," which is what image reconstruction actually needs.

---

## Part 3 — Building the First Pipeline: CSI → Keypoint Heatmap

### 3.1 The plan

The first, simplest version of the idea: take one instant of CSI, and train a small neural
network (explained below) to output an image showing where the 17 body joints are, as soft
glowing dots — called a **heatmap**.

> 📖 **Neural network, encoder, decoder — explained:** a neural network is a stack of
> simple mathematical operations, chained together, that gets *tuned* (via a process called
> training) until it turns a given input into a useful output. Ours is split into two
> halves: an **encoder**, which compresses the messy CSI numbers down into a short
> "summary" (like squeezing a sponge), and a **decoder**, which expands that summary back
> out into an image (like letting the sponge re-expand into a different shape). This
> encoder→decoder pattern is standard for exactly this kind of "turn one kind of data into
> another kind of data" task.


![Pipeline overview](data:image/png;base64,)

*The full pipeline, from WiFi signal to a compared, scored reconstruction.*

### 3.2 Bug #1 — Corrupted CSI frames (NaN values)

The very first thing we noticed: about 6% of CSI files in our data contained
**`NaN`** values ("Not a Number") — essentially blank spots in the data, most likely caused
by dropped WiFi packets during the original recording. Feeding these into training caused
the whole model to output garbage (`NaN`) immediately.

**Fix:** we scanned every file up front, built a list of exactly which frames were affected,
and skipped them. We also added a defensive fallback inside the preprocessing code (replacing
any stray `NaN` with `0`) as a safety net for anything the scan might miss later.

**Why this matters, generally:** real-world sensor data is never perfectly clean. This
wasn't a mistake in our code — it was a mistake to *assume* the data was clean without
checking.

### 3.3 Bug #2 — The hardcoded range that broke almost everything

To draw a heatmap "dot" for a joint, we needed to convert its real-world position (in
meters) into a pixel position on a small image. That conversion needs to know the *range*
of real-world positions to expect — e.g., "everything happens between -0.5m and +0.5m."

We initially picked that range by eyeballing it on one calm, low-movement action
("stretching"). That range turned out to be far too small for high-movement actions like
"jumping" or "kicking" — any joint position outside the assumed range was silently thrown
away by the code. The result: for several actions, the "target" image we were training
against was almost completely black, showing only 1–2 stray dots instead of a full
17-joint skeleton.

**Fix:** instead of guessing, we calculated the real range directly from *all* the actual
position data across every action, and added a small safety margin.

**Why this matters:** this bug didn't crash anything — it just quietly trained the model
against wrong answers. Bugs that don't crash are the most dangerous kind, because nothing
tells you something is wrong.

### 3.4 Bug #3 — The model learning to cheat (output nothing)

Even with correct targets, the very first proper training run got stuck: the loss (a
number measuring "how wrong is the model") stopped improving after one epoch and sat
completely flat.

> 📖 **Epoch, loss — explained:** an *epoch* is one full pass through all the training
> examples. *Loss* is a single number computed after each attempt, summarizing how far off
> the model's guess was from the correct answer; training is the process of nudging the
> model, guess after guess, to make this number smaller.

The cause: a heatmap image is over 85% black background (the joints are small bright
dots on a big empty canvas). A model can get a deceptively good loss score just by
guessing "all black, everywhere" — technically low error, completely useless output.

**Fix:** we changed the loss calculation to penalize mistakes on the *bright* joint pixels
20 times more heavily than mistakes on the black background, forcing the model to actually
try to get the joints right instead of taking the easy way out.

### 3.5 Bug #4 — "It didn't reset" (the stale object problem)

Several times during debugging, we fixed a piece of code, re-ran training, and got
*exactly* the same broken result as before — as if the fix hadn't happened. The cause,
every time: in a notebook environment (where you can run little chunks of code in any
order), editing a function or class doesn't automatically update objects that were already
built from the old version. We had to learn to explicitly rebuild everything, in order,
after any change — or better, design the code so settings live *inside* each object rather
than as loose, easily-stale global values.

### 3.6 The big realization — our "good" result was measuring the wrong thing

After all the above fixes, we got a genuinely confusing result: fixing the coordinate-range
bug (3.3) made the model's score noticeably *worse*, not better. For a while this looked
like a new bug.

It wasn't. Digging back through our own history, we realized the earlier "good" score had
been measured *before* the coordinate-range fix — meaning it was scored against the
broken, mostly-black targets. A model that mostly outputs black scores deceptively well
against a mostly-black answer key. Once the targets were fixed to show full, correct
skeletons, the task became genuinely harder, and the score reflected that honestly.

**The lesson, stated plainly:** *a good-looking score is worthless if you haven't verified
the thing you're comparing against is actually correct.* This idea comes back, bigger,
in Part 4.

### 3.7 First real result

With everything above fixed, this pipeline reached a real, if modest, result:

- **Within the same person** (trained on some of their actions, tested on others):
  reasonable reconstruction — an image-similarity score (SSIM, explained below) around
  **0.18–0.21**.
- **On a completely new person** the model had never seen during training: the result
  **collapsed** — score dropped to about **0.10**, and the model's outputs for very
  different poses became suspiciously similar to each other, a sign it was "hedging"
  toward one generic average guess rather than really reconstructing.

> 📖 **SSIM, PSNR — explained:** these are standard ways to score "how similar are two
> images," used throughout this project. **SSIM** (Structural Similarity Index) ranges
> 0 to 1, where 1 means identical; it tries to measure *structural* similarity, not just
> raw pixel differences. **PSNR** (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio), measured in decibels, is an
> older, simpler measure — higher is better, and it's more sensitive to raw pixel
> differences than to overall structure.

---

## Part 4 — Trying Real Images: Depth

### 4.1 Why switch targets

A 17-dot skeleton is a legitimate but limited stand-in for "an image." We had real,
already-downloaded depth-camera images sitting in the same dataset, so we tried using those
as the target instead — a genuinely denser, more photo-like representation, and a better
match for a project literally titled "image reconstruction."

Before writing any code, we inspected one actual depth file directly rather than assuming
its format — the exact discipline we'd learned the hard way in Part 3. It turned out to be
a 16-bit image (not the more common 8-bit), storing real-world distance in millimeters,
with a value of exactly `0` meaning "no reading" rather than "zero distance." Getting this
detail wrong would have quietly broken every target image, the same class of mistake as
Bug #2 — so this time, we checked first.

### 4.2 A great-looking result that wasn't real

Training on depth images produced an excellent-looking score: **SSIM 0.907**. For a moment,
this looked like a breakthrough.

Then we ran one more check — a **naive baseline**: what score would you get if the "model"
did nothing at all, and simply always guessed the *average* image across the whole training
set, completely ignoring the WiFi signal?

**That naive, do-nothing baseline scored 0.909 — statistically the same as our trained
model.**

This was the single most important check in the whole project. The room's background
(walls, floor, furniture) is identical in almost every frame and takes up most of the
image; the person is a comparatively small moving part. A model can score very well just
by learning "always output roughly this room," without learning anything about the *person*
at all — exactly the same shortcut as Bug #3, just hidden better this time because the
background isn't plain black, so the collapse wasn't obvious to the eye.

**Lesson:** always compare against a "do-nothing" baseline before trusting a good-looking
score. It's the single cheapest, most revealing check available.

### 4.3 A sharper diagnostic: residual correlation

To get past this, we built a stricter test: instead of comparing the *whole* image, compare
only the model's *deviation* from the average image against the *true* deviation for that
frame. If the model has really learned something about the specific person in each frame,
this "deviation-from-average" should line up between prediction and reality. If it hasn't,
this number should sit right around zero.

For the single-frame depth model: **-0.028** — essentially zero. Confirmed: the model had
learned nothing about the person at all, across two entirely different target
representations now (keypoints and depth). That consistency across representations
strongly suggested the bottleneck wasn't the target image type — it was the *input*.

---

## Part 5 — Chasing the Real Signal: Giving the Model Time

### 5.1 The hypothesis

Every experiment so far fed the model **one isolated instant** of CSI — about 10 rapid
samples, covering a tiny fraction of a second. Real movement takes time to show up in a
signal. If pose information lives in *how the signal is changing*, a single frozen snapshot
might simply never contain it, no matter how good the model or target image is.

**Test:** instead of one CSI frame, stack several *consecutive* frames together as input,
giving the model a short window of time to look at instead of a single instant.

### 5.2 The results: a real, if surprising, curve


![N_FRAMES sweep](data:image/png;base64,)

*Residual correlation (the "does the model see the person at all" score) as the size of
the input time-window changes, tested on a single person's data.*

Stacking 5 consecutive frames immediately produced a real, positive signal
(**+0.171**, up from essentially zero). Stretching further to 11 frames improved it
slightly more, to a peak of **+0.197**. But pushing to 15 frames made it *worse* again
(**+0.119**) — not a straight line of "more is better."

We identified two likely, non-exclusive reasons for the drop at 15 frames:

1. **More input channels, same training budget:** stacking more frames means a bigger
   first layer in the network, which is harder to train well in a fixed number of epochs
   without adjusting other settings.
2. **A stricter safety rule was quietly shrinking the training set:** our rule at the time
   was "if *any* frame in the window is corrupted, throw out the whole sample." With bigger
   windows, that rule throws away a lot more data — at 11 frames, this discarded roughly
   **37–45%** of all possible samples. (We later relaxed this rule; see Part 6.3.)

---

## Part 6 — The Real Breakthrough: More People, Not Just More Time

### 6.1 Leave-one-subject-out: the harder, more honest test

So far, "testing on a new person" and "testing with more temporal context" had only been
tried separately. We combined them: train on four people's data pooled together, then test
on a **fifth person the model had never seen at all** — the realistic scenario for any
system that would ever be used on someone new.

### 6.2 The result

This produced the strongest result of the entire project:

- Residual correlation jumped to **+0.324** — nearly double the best single-person result.
- For the first time, SSIM itself (not just the more sensitive residual check) showed a
  real, if modest, edge over the naive baseline (0.918 vs. 0.912).
- The gap between "how similar are two different predictions" and "how similar are the two
  *true* images" — our test for whether the model was hedging toward one generic answer —
  shrank to its smallest point yet.

**Interpretation:** pooling more people's data gave the model enough real variety to
actually learn the underlying CSI-to-shape relationship, rather than just memorizing one
person's specific signal quirks. This suggests the earlier cross-subject collapse (Part 3.7)
wasn't proof that this task is impossible — it was, at least partly, a symptom of not having
enough training data and not enough temporal context, tackled together.

### 6.3 One more fix: relaxing the "throw out the whole window" rule

We revisited the strict corruption rule from Part 5.2. Instead of discarding a sample if
*any* frame in its window was corrupted, we only discarded it if the **center** frame
(the one the target image is actually matched to) was bad — letting the existing
NaN-safety code quietly clean up any merely-nearby corrupted frames instead of throwing
the whole sample away.

This recovered a large amount of previously-discarded training data, and pushed the result
to its final, best value: **+0.363**.


![Final progression](data:image/png;base64,)

*The complete progression across every major fix, on the same scale, showing how each
change compounded on the last.*

### 6.4 What this final number actually means, honestly

+0.363 is a real, positive, carefully-verified signal — not a fluke, and not a metric
artifact, since it survived the same rigorous baseline-and-residual checks that caught
every previous false positive in this project. It is **not** a strong enough result to
claim "this reliably reconstructs what a stranger looks like from WiFi alone." It's exactly
what it looks like: solid evidence that the information exists and is learnable, at a
modest strength, under these specific conditions (this hardware, this room, this amount of
data, this window size).

---

## Part 7 — The Engineering Lessons (Not Specific to Machine Learning)

A few problems came up more than once, in different disguises, and are worth naming
directly since they'll show up in almost any similar project:

- **Stale state in notebooks.** Editing code above doesn't retroactively fix objects
  already built below it. When in doubt, restart everything and re-run top to bottom.
- **Silent bugs are worse than crashes.** Every genuinely time-consuming bug in this
  project (the coordinate range, the sparsity collapse, the depth-baseline illusion) ran
  *without error messages* — the code executed fine and produced a plausible-looking wrong
  answer. Crashes are annoying; silent wrong answers are dangerous.
- **Always build a "do-nothing" comparison.** This one idea (Part 4.2) caught more real
  problems than any other single technique in the whole project.
- **Verify a file's actual format before writing code against it.** Both the coordinate
  range bug and the depth-image work were only handled correctly because we eventually
  adopted the habit of inspecting one real file directly, instead of assuming a format
  from documentation or intuition.
- **Environment issues aren't always your fault.** Partway through, training failed with a
  cryptic CUDA error — which turned out to be a known, already-reported bug in the cloud
  platform itself (an older GPU model no longer supported by the installed software),
  fixed simply by switching to a different, supported GPU option.
- **Redundant work hides in "obviously fine" code.** Loading overlapping windows of frames
  from disk one sample at a time silently re-read and reprocessed the same files many times
  over; caching each file's processed result once cut a multi-hour run down dramatically.

## Part 8 — What We Actually Found (Full Summary Table)

| Stage | What changed | Residual correlation | Honest verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keypoints, within-subject | first working pipeline | — (SSIM 0.18–0.21) | real, modest signal |
| Keypoints, new person | same model, unseen subject | — (SSIM ~0.10) | collapses |
| Depth, single frame | denser real-image target | -0.028 | **no real signal** — caught by baseline check |
| Depth, 5-frame window | added short temporal context | +0.171 | real signal appears |
| Depth, 11-frame window | more temporal context | +0.197 | best single-person result |
| Depth, 15-frame window | even more context | +0.119 | signal drops — data loss + harder optimization |
| Depth, 11-frame, 4 people→new person | pooled training data | +0.324 | biggest single jump in the project |
| Depth, 11-frame, 4 people, relaxed data rule | recovered lost training samples | **+0.363** | **final, best, most defensible result** |

---

## Part 9 — What We Missed, and Said So Honestly

- **Image resolution was capped at 64×64 pixels** for every experiment, to keep
  comparisons fair across representations. This puts a hard ceiling on how much fine detail
  (limb position, precise pose) could ever be recovered — the model was always working with
  a coarse, blurry target, never a sharp one.
- **We did not go into this having read the relevant research literature first.** This
  project was built empirically — try something, measure honestly, follow what the data
  says — rather than starting from a deep survey of prior published work. That's a
  legitimate way to build a first project, but it means some of our "discoveries" (like
  needing temporal context, or that raw end-to-end reconstruction is hard) are things
  published researchers had already found and built more sophisticated solutions around.
  Part 10 covers this directly.
- **Every configuration was only run once.** Neural network training has some inherent
  randomness; a single run can't fully separate "this setting is genuinely better" from
  "this run got lucky." A rigorous version of this project would repeat each configuration
  several times and report an average with a range, not a single number.
- **We didn't use every sensor available.** MM-Fi also includes radar (mmWave) and LiDAR
  point-cloud data, and full anonymized color photos, none of which were used here.
- **The 15-frame dip was never fully separated into its two possible causes** (harder
  optimization vs. lost training data) — we have evidence pointing at both, not a clean
  answer for which mattered more.

---

## Part 10 — What We'd Add Next: Learning From the Research We Skipped

After finishing the experiments above, we looked at how published researchers have tackled
this same problem, and found a clear, informative progression:

| Year | Work | What it outputs | Core idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 | CSI2Image | RGB image | A simple generator network, optionally paired with a second "critic" network (a GAN) |
| 2024 | Through-Wall Imaging (a.k.a. "WiFiCam") | RGB image | A more advanced generative model (MoPoE-VAE) combining several sensor types |
| 2025 | Wi-Depth | Depth image | A generative model that is *also* trained to separately predict the person's shape, depth, and position as side-tasks, not just the final image |
| 2025 | LatentCSI | RGB image | Maps CSI directly into the internal "imagination space" of a large, already-trained image-generation AI (Stable Diffusion), letting that pretrained model fill in realistic detail |

**The reassuring part:** Wi-Depth's core idea — that asking a model to predict the final
image *and* some simpler, more directly physical facts (like "where is the person's
center") at the same time helps it learn faster — is basically a more sophisticated,
published version of the exact intuition our own Part 5 and Part 6 experiments arrived at
independently: a plain, single-task model really struggles with this problem, and giving it
more to work with (temporal context, more people's worth of data) is what actually helped.
We didn't set out to reproduce Wi-Depth's insight, but our results ended up supporting it
anyway. That's a good sign that the underlying difficulty we ran into is real and shared,
not an artifact of a mistake in our own setup.

### Proposed next step: an auxiliary task, not a full rebuild

Rather than attempting a full rebuild toward LatentCSI's approach (which leans on a large
pretrained image-generation model and a substantially heavier training setup), a much
smaller, directly actionable next step — borrowed from Wi-Depth's simpler idea — is
achievable with what we already have:

**Add a second, small output to the existing best model that predicts the person's
approximate center position** (easily computed from the same `ground_truth.npy` keypoint
files already on hand), trained *alongside* the existing depth-image output, not instead of
it. The two tasks share the same encoder, so the position-prediction task acts as an extra,
more direct hint that nudges the model toward actually locating the person — rather than
relying solely on the harder, noisier full-image reconstruction loss to teach it that on
its own.

This is a modest, well-motivated, low-risk addition: it reuses data already downloaded, it
builds on the exact model architecture already validated and understood, and it's directly
inspired by a real, current (2025) published result rather than a guess — while
deliberately avoiding a much larger, riskier rebuild (a full generative/diffusion pipeline)
that this project's timeline and current findings don't yet justify.

---

## Glossary — Every Technical Term Used Above, in Plain Language

- **CSI (Channel State Information):** a detailed record of how a WiFi signal's strength
  and timing changed while traveling through a room.
- **Amplitude:** signal strength (like volume).
- **Phase:** signal timing shift (like whether a wave arrived early or late).
- **Subcarrier:** one of many mini-frequencies WiFi splits its data across; CSI is measured
  separately on each one.
- **Neural network:** a tunable chain of simple math operations that learns to turn an
  input into a useful output through repeated practice on examples.
- **Encoder / Decoder:** the two halves of our network — the encoder compresses input data
  down to a short summary; the decoder expands that summary back into an image.
- **Epoch:** one full pass through every training example.
- **Loss:** a single number scoring how wrong a model's output was; training tries to make
  this number smaller over time.
- **NaN ("Not a Number"):** a placeholder value marking missing or corrupted data.
- **Heatmap:** an image where brightness shows "how likely/strong something is" at each
  spot — used here to mark joint positions as soft glowing dots.
- **SSIM (Structural Similarity Index):** a 0-to-1 score measuring how structurally similar
  two images are; 1 means identical.
- **PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio):** a decibel score measuring pixel-level similarity
  between two images; higher is better.
- **Overfitting:** when a model starts memorizing quirks of its specific training examples
  instead of learning something that generalizes to new, unseen examples.
- **Naive / do-nothing baseline:** the score you'd get from the simplest possible
  non-strategy (e.g., always guessing the average answer), used as a sanity check against
  a model's "real" performance.
- **Residual:** how much an actual value differs from some reference (here, from the
  average image) — used to isolate the *interesting*, person-specific part of an image
  from the boring, shared background.
- **GAN (Generative Adversarial Network):** a setup with two competing networks — one
  generates fake outputs, the other tries to catch them — that improve by competing
  against each other.
- **VAE (Variational Autoencoder):** a type of encoder/decoder network with a built-in
  randomness component, commonly used for generating varied, realistic-looking outputs.
- **Latent space:** the internal, compressed "summary" representation a model uses
  partway through processing — not directly human-readable, but where a lot of a model's
  "understanding" effectively lives.
- **Diffusion model:** a modern class of image-generation AI that creates images by
  starting from random noise and gradually refining it into a coherent picture.
- **Auxiliary task:** an extra, usually simpler prediction target trained alongside the
  main goal, used to give a model additional, more direct learning signal.

---

*This document reflects the project's process and findings as of the final experiment
described above (multi-subject, 11-frame temporal window, relaxed data-filtering rule,
residual correlation +0.363). It is written to explain the work honestly — including every
false start — rather than to present only the polished final result.*
